abstract:
Maternal thyroid peroxidase antibody (TPOAb) positivity increases offspring neurodevelopmental risk, but the underlying pathogenic mechanisms remain incompletely defined.
We combined mouse experiments and human cohort analyses to investigate the effects of maternal TPOAb exposure. Mice offspring were assessed for maternal antibody transmission, placental pathology, blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, neuroinflammation, and neurotrophic/synaptic signaling pathways. Human data were used to examine the mediating role of placental inflammatory factors in the association between maternal TPOAb positivity and offspring cognitive function.
Through mouse experiments, we observed that in utero TPOAb exposure resulted in sustained high maternal antibody levels and was associated with transplacental passage. This exposure was associated with significant placental pathology, including reduced placental volume, diminished vascularity, and upregulated expression of inflammatory cytokines. TPOAb was detectable in the fetal circulation and brain parenchyma. Offspring exhibited BBB disruption (reduced claudin-5, occludin, and ZO-1 protein expression) and persistent hippocampal neuroinflammation accompanied by morphological evidence of microglial activation and altered bulk hippocampal expression of the myeloid-associated markers CD16 and CD206. Despite unaltered neuronal density, sustained alterations in brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)/tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) and synaptic signaling pathways (PSD-95, synapsin-1, CREB) were observed. In an exploratory mediation analysis of the human cohort, placental inflammatory factors statistically accounted for 9.9-25.7% of the association between maternal TPOAb positivity and offspring cognitive function, consistent with partial mediation.
These findings suggest a placenta-dependent pathway whereby maternal TPOAb positivity is associated with placental inflammation and antibody transfer, followed by fetal BBB compromise, persistent microglial activation, and altered neurotrophic and synaptic signaling, collectively contributing to offspring neurodevelopmental risk.
